nameStory: The 'cudweed' name comes from this plant's traditional use as a soft, woolly bedding for livestock - farmers would gather its fuzzy stems and leaves to create comfortable 'cud' for their animals to rest on. The 'marsh' part tells you exactly where to look for it: in damp, soggy spots where few other plants want to grow.
description: Marsh cudweed is a small, low-growing annual plant that hugs the ground in wet, disturbed areas. It rarely grows taller than 6 inches, forming spreading mats of grayish-green, woolly stems and leaves. The entire plant has a soft, fuzzy texture that feels almost cotton-like to the touch. Its tiny flowers are clustered in small, inconspicuous heads that blend into the overall gray-green appearance of the plant.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall with branching stems that feel soft and woolly to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves covered in dense, gray-white woolly hairs that give them a feltlike texture and silvery appearance

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous flower heads clustered at stem tips and leaf joints, appearing brownish-yellow and easily overlooked among the woolly foliage

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels remarkably soft and woolly, like touching cotton batting or felt fabric

habitat: Look for marsh cudweed in damp, disturbed ground throughout New England - muddy farm tracks, wet field edges, pond margins, and acidic soils that stay moist. It thrives in areas where the soil has been compacted or churned up, like along hiking trails through wetlands or in farm gateways where water collects.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small, woolly rosettes in damp soil, already showing their characteristic fuzzy texture even when tiny.
seasonality.summer: Plants spread into full mats and produce their small flower clusters from mid to late summer, though blooms are easily missed.
seasonality.fall: Seeds disperse and plants begin to die back, leaving behind dried, still-woolly stems that persist for a while.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants have died completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'marsh' cudweed, this little plant is actually a brilliant opportunist - it can complete its entire life cycle in temporary puddles that only exist for a few months, growing from seed to mature plant and back to seed faster than most plants can even get established!
confusionNotes: The woolly, gray-green appearance might remind you of lamb's ear or other fuzzy garden plants, but marsh cudweed's tiny size, ground-hugging habit, and preference for muddy, disturbed spots (not garden beds) quickly set it apart. Remember: if it's growing in a neat garden, it's probably not marsh cudweed!
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this with the more famous 'cudweed' used in herbal medicine - that's usually referring to other species in the same genus. While marsh cudweed was historically used for animal bedding, it's the least showy member of a family that includes sunflowers and daisies, proving that not all Asteraceae family members are garden showstoppers.
compareHints: Since marsh cudweed is the only cudweed species commonly found in New England wetlands, compare it to other small, mat-forming plants in wet areas. Unlike pearlwort or other tiny marsh plants, cudweed's distinctive woolly texture and gray-green color make it unique - no other small wetland plant feels quite so much like touching a cotton ball.
